newsitem.title: FRANCE: French state bank says more state aid only way out.
newsitem.headline: French state bank says more state aid only way out.

text.p: The boss of Credit Lyonnais told French taxpayers on Friday their lone hope of recouping some of the billions of francs of public money shovelled into the state-owned bank was by pumping in more and privatising it.

"It's in the taxpayers' interest and in the state's interest to privatise the bank in the best way possible, at the best price possible, to erase part of the bill," Jean Peyrelevade, chairman of Credit Lyonnais, said in a radio interview.

A day earlier the French had learned that the bank, whose plight ranks as France's worst banking horror story, needed to raid their wallets yet again -- this time to be recapitalised to prepare it for privatisation.

One newspaper, Liberation -- under the front-page banner headline "Should This Bank Be Saved?" -- estimated on Friday that the ultimate bill to taxpayers from the bank's reckless expansion spree during the 1980s could hit 150 billion francs ($29 billion).

The bank, announcing a modest 67 million franc first-half profit, said late on Thursday its balance sheet would need an injection of at least eight to nine billion francs to attract a buyer and achieve the government's goal of rapid privatisation.

That recapitalisation would be on top of 3.9 billion francs of emergency state aid announced last week to repair what turned out to be overly harsh terms of a state salvage last year that would have driven the bank back into the red.

The bank's warning that it would need to be recapitalised was not a big surprise. In announcing last week's aid, the government accelerated the privatisation timetable from the year 2000 and said the bank would need another full-scale bailout -- the third in the three years -- to prepare it for sale.
The government has not said how much it would pump into the bank but the press has been speculating on at least 10 billion francs, close to the amount the bank says may be needed.

The latest sums, however, are small when compared with losses of at least 90 billion francs expected on the sale of the bank's dud assets amassed during its expansion binge and now housed in a separate, so-called "bad bank".
Credit Lyonnais, once France's flagship bank, rocketed in size during the late 1980s, then came crashing to earth in the early 1990s when property values collapsed and economic growth evaporated.
Peyrelevade on Friday defended the need for public money to boost the bank's balance sheet, saying rival Banque Nationale de Paris was recapitalised by the state before privatisation.
"When you recapitalise, you raise the sale price," he said. "What you pay now you should get back when you sell."

He said the key to making the bank saleable was boosting its Cooke ratio, an international banking solvency standard measuring capital to liabilities, currently 4.5 percent, by at least one percentage point. He estimated it would cost eight to nine billion francs to raise the ratio to 5.5 percent.
But he cast strong doubt on the government's aim of a swift privatisation and sources close to the bank said no sale was expected until at least early 1998.

The bank must first prepare a privatisation plan which it has pledged by the year-end. In that, it will identify which non-strategic assets to sell to appease the European Commission, which will have to approve fresh state money.

It must also improve weak profitability in its core French market, an uphill task in the country's depressed banking climate, where margins are among the world's lowest. Its first half banking income fell 5.8 percent in France.
The bank eked out a 13 million franc profit in 1995 after racking up 21 billion francs in losses between 1992 and 1994.

So far, the bank's rivals, which attacked the previous state rescues, have been silent. Societe Generale chairman Marc Vienot, a sharp critic, said recently he would keep quiet, commenting: "They accused me of firing on an ambulance. I won't now shoot at a hearse."

Whatever happens, it seems certain the bank will lose its independence, falling into either the hands of a foreign buyer or being taken over by a domestic rival -- a humbling fate for an institution that was once the world's biggest bank outside Japan. ($1=5.178 French Franc)
